title: Shiva's drum
hook: Shiva's drum at the end of his dance, the sounds that fell out of it, and why Hindus treat the word itself as holy
carry: shabda brahman: the word itself is sacred
tomorrow: why do some families leave one seat empty at a Ramayana reading?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Krishna taught, then left the choice to Arjuna, and Arjuna stood. Today, a story about where the list of Sanskrit's sounds came from. It starts with a drum.
screen: `KRISHNA LEAVES THE CHOICE TO ARJUNA.` · `WHERE THE SOUNDS CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: Plenty of songs start with a drummer clicking the sticks: one, two, three, four, and the whole band knows where to come in. Here's an old story with a count-in of its own. Shiva, as Nataraja, the lord of dance, is finishing his dance. Sages stand around him, waiting for something they can't name yet. As the dance ends, he lifts his small drum and strikes it. Again. Again. The verse that tells this even counts the beats: nine times, and five times. And each beat comes out as a cluster of sounds. What are they for?
screen: `ONE, TWO, THREE, FOUR.` → `SHIVA FINISHES HIS DANCE.` → `NINE BEATS, AND FIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's what the beats were, as tradition tells it. Short strings of letters. A, i, u, with a marker at the end. Then the other vowels, and on through the consonants to the very last one, ha. They're called the Shiva Sutras, the threads of Shiva, and they sit at the head of Panini's grammar, grouped so cleverly that one short word, ac, names every vowel. Tradition says Panini received them from the drum. Now, why would a grammar want a god's drum at its start? Because in Hindu thought, sound isn't only a tool for pointing at holy things. It can be holy itself. About fifteen hundred years ago, the grammarian Bhartrihari opened his great book on language with a bold line: Brahman, the reality with no beginning and no end, is in its very nature the Word, and the whole world unfolds from it. Teachers call this shabda brahman, the Word as the divine. It's why a mantra is handled with such care, why chanters guard every syllable, and why a grandmother wants even a short line learned well. The drum story says the same thing in a picture: before the rules, before the world, a sound. And the sages around Shiva didn't get a book. They got a rhythm, and had to listen.
screen: `THE SHIVA SUTRAS, OFF THE DRUM.` · `AC: EVERY VOWEL IN ONE WORD.` · `BHARTRIHARI: BRAHMAN IS THE WORD.` · `SHABDA BRAHMAN: SOUND AS HOLY.` · then, large: `FIRST, A SOUND.`

segments.voice: If you know a short mantra, like Om namah shivaya, say it once aloud, slowly, and listen to each sound as if the sound itself were the gift. If you don't pray, tap a slow beat with one finger and listen only to that sound, where it starts and how it fades. Then stop, and listen to the quiet the last one leaves.
The sounds: today, the ones tradition says fell from Shiva's drum, and the Hindu teaching that the word itself is sacred.
Something to keep: shabda brahman, the word itself is sacred. Before any rule, there was a sound. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Students of Panini's grammar learn the Shiva Sutras by heart, usually by reciting them aloud, and the story of Shiva's drum is told as the origin of the list; mantras are chanted with great care because the sound itself is held to be sacred.

Written fresh in v3. Days 1439-1442 ('the sounds') were not on disk when this was written, so the angle (Shiva's drum and the Shiva Sutras) could not be checked against them; please make sure it doesn't repeat one of those days.

The drum story: Nandikeshvara's Kashika, opening verse (nrittavasane natarajarajo nanada dhakkam navapanchavaram...). The 'nine and five times' count is the verse's own. The tradition that Panini received the sutras from the drum is popular tradition; the script says 'tradition says'. Confirm.
ac (a ... c in 'ai au c') = all vowels; hal (ha ... l, the last sutra) = all consonants; Ashtadhyayi 1.1.71 for how the abbreviations work. Confirm the plain-English description.

Priya storyline (days 1443-1456): she says yes to reading one Sanskrit line at her school's senior send-off; Nani picks the line (vasudhaiva kutumbakam, introduced day 1446), she learns its sounds and joins, and says it on day 1456.
